title: Critical Data Question 1
scenario: The Arctic is one of Earth's polar regions. Orcas, Narwhals, Spotted Seals, Sea Otters and Polar bears all live here.
question: Where is the Arctic located?
imageSource: Image source - NOC Arctic Cruise & Pexels

options.text: At the south (bottom) of the planet.
options.explanation: The south polar region is called the Antarctic.

options.text: At the north (top) of the planet.
options.explanation: The Arctic is Earth's northern polar region. It's around the North Pole.

options.text: At the equator (around the middle of the planet).
options.explanation: The Equator is the warm middle line around Earth. It's far from the polar Arctic region.

title: Critical Data Question 2
scenario: The Arctic and Antarctic are both cold polar regions, but they are not the same kind of place.
question: What makes the the Arctic different?
imageSource: Image source - Sergey Torbik & The Shuttervision (Pexels)

options.explanation: The Arctic is not a continent. Antarctica is a continent.

options.text: A cold ocean surrounded by land.
options.explanation: The Arctic is the Arctic Ocean, covered by sea ice and surrounded by northern land areas.
The Arctic is not land, on an ocean. It's ocean covered by sea ice. Penguins only live in Antarctica, not the Arctic!

title: Critical Data Question 3
scenario: Scientists can study Arctic sea ice over many years by observing it from above.
question: On our 3d Map Model, how did was the sea-ice age data collected? Hint: Click on the icon in the right corner of the screen to go back to the map and have a look to see if you can find the answer!
imageSource: Image source - Igor Mashkov & Zelch Csaba (Pexels)

options.explanation: A measuring tape cannot measure sea-ice age across the whole Arctic Ocean.

options.text: From satellites looking at the ocean.
options.explanation: Satellites observe sea ice from space, helping scientists map and track changes across the Arctic Ocean.
Laboratory work can help study samples! Large-scale sea-ice age data has to be collected using technology.

title: Critical Data Question 4
scenario: Arctic sea ice grows during the cold dark winter and melts during the warmer summer.
question: Which month has the most sea ice?

options.explanation: Arctic sea ice usually reaches its yearly maximum around March, after the winter freezing season.
By June, the Arctic has entered the melt season, so sea ice is usually decreasing.
October is after the summer low, when sea ice starts growing again. But it is not usually the maximum month.

title: Critical Data Question 5
scenario: As white Arctic ice melts, it reveals dark ocean water underneath.
question: How does this change affect the amount of sunlight the Earth absorbs?
imageSource: Image source - Star Zhang & Sergey Guk (Pexels)

options.text: The dark water reflects more sunlight, cooling the planet.
options.explanation: It's actually the reverse. Think about dark clothes in warm weather - they attract more heat.

options.text: The dark water absorbs more sunlight, warming the planet faster.
options.explanation: That's right! Water absorbs more sunlight because it's so dark. Ice is very bright - and so it reflects more light than dark water.

options.text: It has no effect because the sun's strength stays the same.
options.explanation: That's incorrect as this ignores the Albedo Effect (how shiny or dark a surface is and how much light it reflects back).
